title: Rerunning GPT-1's Training Would Cost Less Than ChatGPT Plus

The New York Times counted how much math it takes to build a frontier model. OpenAI’s own price list shows how fast that math spoils.

The short answer: GPT-6 Astra took about 940 septillion calculations to train, which at the price per calculation Epoch AI used for Grok 4 works out to roughly $920 million. The number that decides whether that spend pays off is not the size of the bill. It is how long the model stays worth full price, and in 2026 OpenAI’s own catalog says that window is about two months.

Here is a fun way to feel how fast AI math gets cheap. GPT-1, OpenAI’s first model in the series, took 18 million trillion calculations to train in 2018. Priced at what a calculation costs to rent today, that entire training run comes to about $18. Less than one month of ChatGPT Plus.

The Times ran a gorgeous interactive on October 15 about the other end of that curve: GPT-6 Astra, trained on nearly an octillion calculations, more than 50 million times GPT-1’s bill. The piece leans on stars in the universe and molecules in the human body to make the number land.

Fair enough. But the octillion is the wrong number to stare at if you run a business. A frontier model is a product with a sell-by date, and the date is printed in OpenAI’s own pricing table. Below: the arithmetic of what Astra cost, how long it has to earn it back, and why the best business in AI might be the one that never sells the model at all.

## What Happened

Aatish Bhatia’s piece for The Upshot walks through OpenAI’s GPT series by training compute, using estimates from Epoch AI, the research group that tracks AI scaling. The ladder is steep:

- GPT-1 (2018): 18 million trillion calculations
- GPT-2 (2019): nearly 300 times that
- GPT-3.5 (2022): over 140,000 times GPT-1
- GPT-4 (2023): over a million times GPT-1
- GPT-6 Astra (2026): nearly an octillion, more than 50 million times GPT-1

The Times also gives the one dollar figure anyone can anchor on. Epoch estimates that training xAI’s Grok 4 took roughly 500 septillion calculations and cost about $490 million in hardware and electricity, plus emissions equal to roughly 150,000 tons of carbon dioxide.

Divide one by the other and you get the going rate for frontier math: about $0.98 per quintillion calculations. That single ratio unlocks everything else in this piece.

Epoch’s model database puts Astra at 9.4e26 calculations, trained on Nvidia GB200 chips and released September 3, 2026. At the Grok 4 rate, that is about $921 million. Run the same rate backward:

- GPT-1: about $18
- GPT-2: about $4,900
- GPT-3.5: about $2.5 million
- GPT-4: about $21 million
- GPT-6 Astra: about $921 million

The GPT-4 line is the tell. Sam Altman said in 2023 that GPT-4 cost more than $100 million to train. Rerun those same calculations at today’s rate and the bill is roughly a fifth of that. Same math, same result, under three years later. That is what depreciation looks like when the asset is a capability.

## The Backstory

Every exhibit in the Times piece measures the cost of producing intelligence. None measures how long the product stays valuable once it ships. That second clock is the one that runs the business, and OpenAI has been publishing it all year, one price change at a time.

Here is the 2026 flagship calendar:

- GPT-5.4 shipped March 5
- GPT-5.5 shipped April 23, 49 days later
- GPT-5.6 shipped July 9, 77 days later
- GPT-6 Astra shipped September 3, 56 days later

That is an average of about 61 days between flagships. Two months at the top, then a successor.

Now watch what happened to GPT-5.6 inside its own 56 days. It launched as three tiers, which we covered at the time as a pricing ladder aimed squarely at Anthropic: Sol at $5 input and $30 output per million tokens, Terra at $2.50 and $15, Luna at $1 and $6.

- Day 21 (July 30): Terra cut 20% and Luna cut 80%, both permanently. Luna’s input price went from $1.00 to $0.20.
- Day 43 (August 21): Sol, the flagship, cut to $4 input and $20 output, a 33% drop on output, billed as a promotion running at least through November 21.
- Day 56 (September 3): GPT-6 Astra ships at $10 input and $50 output, exactly 2.5 times Sol’s new price on both lines.

Launch, markdown, successor. Eight weeks. If you have ever worked in apparel retail, you know this rhythm. It is how a store clears last season’s racks before the new collection lands.

## The Plan

Retailers mark down because inventory loses value with time. The question is whether AI capability loses value that fast too. Epoch AI answered it on September 22 in a report titled “The plunging price of thought,” by Luke Emberson and David Roodman.

Their headline finding: since 2023, the cost of reaching a fixed level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter, or roughly 13 times a year. Epoch ranks that ahead of DNA sequencing, computing and lithium batteries in their historical runs.

The more important number sits one layer down. For a performance level that has just reached the state of the art, the decline is steeper, about 66% per quarter, or 75 times a year. Two years after debut, the pace slows to about 32% per quarter.

Convert 66% a quarter into a half-life and you get about 59 days. Fresh frontier capability gets half as expensive to match roughly every eight weeks.

Put those two clocks side by side. OpenAI ships a flagship about every 61 days. The cost of matching a new frontier level halves about every 59. The price list and the capability curve are running on the same schedule, and that is not a coincidence. The markdown is the market telling OpenAI what its own inventory is worth.

Which brings us to the payback math nobody in the Times piece ran.

If Astra cost roughly $921 million to train and holds the flagship slot for about 61 days, the training bill works out to about $15 million for every day at the top.

That figure has a twin in the same article. The Times reports that OpenAI’s agents, working on Millennium Prize math problems over five days in September, generated output that would cost about $15 million at Astra’s public rates. That checks out: OpenAI disclosed about 300 billion output tokens for the run, and 300 billion at $50 per million is $15 million. We dug into what that run produced, and why the prize committee cannot even start counting for two years, in our Navier-Stokes piece.

So here is the picture. To earn back its training before a successor arrives, Astra has to bill the equivalent of that entire five-day research push, at full list price, every single day it is the flagship. And it has to do it while its own predecessor sells output at 40% of Astra’s price.

## The Business Model Angle

Training is a perishable cost of goods, not a capital asset. Accountants would love to treat an octillion calculations like a factory with a 20-year life. The price list says it is closer to fresh fish. The economic life of a frontier model is set by the next model’s launch date, and the lab sets that date itself.

The real moat is the shelf, not the fish. ChatGPT Plus has cost $20 a month since February 2023. Across that span the model underneath changed many times, and the price on the storefront never moved. The subscription turns a perishable product into a non-perishable one. The API customer pays for a specific model and watches it get marked down. The subscriber pays for “the best model, whatever it is this month,” and that promise does not depreciate. We have written about the catch: the model, not the customer, decides how many tokens each answer burns.

Agents are the amortization schedule. The Times notes that inference costs are rising because reasoning models and agents generate far more text per task. Read that from the seller’s side. A model with a two-month window has to be pushed through as many tokens as possible before it spoils. Agents that loop for hours are the fastest way to sell a lot of fish quickly.

Followers are buying last season’s racks. If matching a new frontier level gets 75 times cheaper in a year, the second-place lab is not losing a race. It is buying the same capability at a clearance price. That is the cheapest position in the market, and it is why OpenAI’s commitments keep outrunning its revenue while cheaper rivals keep closing the gap.

Picks-and-shovels sellers get paid either way. Every 61-day cycle is a fresh order for chips, power and data center space. Whoever sells the calculations collects on every model, including the ones that go on sale in week six. We tracked how that shows up in Nvidia’s revenue per gigawatt.

## The Risk

The case against this reading is real, so here it is at full strength.

The model is not the asset. The lab is. Each training run teaches the team how to run the next one, and new models build on data, code and techniques from the last. A pharmaceutical company does not write off its research platform when one drug goes generic. By that logic the $921 million buys a capability that carries forward, and the 61-day window measures one product, not the investment.

Old models keep earning. Sol did not disappear on September 3. It is still on the price list, still serving customers at $4 and $20. A model that loses the flagship slot becomes a cheaper tier with a long tail of revenue. The $15 million a day figure assumes the flagship has to pay for itself alone, which overstates the pressure.

The cost estimate is a rough order of magnitude. The $921 million applies Grok 4’s price per calculation to Astra. Astra trained on newer GB200 chips, which deliver more calculations per dollar than the H100 hours Epoch priced for Grok 4, so the true compute bill is probably lower. But Epoch itself says its Grok 4 figure leaves out experiments, staff and serving costs, which push the real total higher. The two errors point in opposite directions. Treat the figure as “around a billion dollars,” not as an invoice.

Scale fixes a lot. The OpenAI spokesperson quoted by the Times makes the amortization argument directly, saying “each training investment benefits more people as adoption grows.” A fixed cost spread across hundreds of millions of users can look small per person. That is true, and it is exactly why the subscription business matters more than the API.

The cadence could slow. If bigger training runs take longer, flagships may stay on top for longer than two months. The Times notes the power needed to train the largest models has doubled every year. A longer build could stretch the window, at the price of a bigger bill.

## Quick Questions

How much did GPT-6 Astra cost to train? OpenAI has not said. Applying Epoch AI’s Grok 4 estimate of about $0.98 per quintillion calculations to Epoch’s figure of 9.4e26 calculations for Astra gives roughly $921 million, with real uncertainty in both directions.

Why would GPT-1’s training cost only $18? Because the price of a calculation has collapsed. GPT-1 needed 18 million trillion calculations. At about $0.98 per quintillion, that is about $18.

Did OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 prices before GPT-6 shipped? Yes. Terra and Luna were cut permanently on July 30, and Sol was cut 20% on input and 33% on output on August 21 as a promotion running at least through November 21. GPT-6 Astra launched September 3.

How fast does AI capability get cheaper? Epoch AI estimates about 47% per quarter at a fixed performance level, and about 66% per quarter for a level that has just reached the frontier.

Is ChatGPT Plus getting more expensive? No. It has been $20 a month since February 2023. What has changed is the model behind it, which OpenAI swaps without changing the price.

## The Business Model Analyst Take

The Times asked what data centers are doing, and the answer is a mind-boggling amount of math. True. But in business terms, they are doing something more familiar. They are manufacturing inventory with an eight-week shelf life.
